reuse_evidence: FULLY FRESH. NO CORPUS COVERAGE. A scan of every built specification for charterparty content returns no question on the charterer's influence on machinery operation. The highest-scoring hits are the CII questions (QP2508-Q2, QP2509-Q2, QP2602-Q2), where 'time charter' and 'charterparty clause' appear only as the commercial vehicle for carbon-intensity liability - an adjacent commercial topic, not this examiner's task. The remaining hits are single incidental mentions inside Big Data, IoT, operating-cost and LLMC questions.

THE ADJACENT MATERIAL WAS DELIBERATELY NOT MINED. The CII questions discuss how charterparty clauses allocate responsibility for a ship's carbon rating. This stem asks how a charterer's employment orders affect the operation of propulsion and auxiliary machinery, and what a Chief Engineer does about a breakdown history before sailing. Sharing the phrase 'time charter' is not sharing a task, and importing CII material would have answered a question that was not set.

THE ONE THING CARRIED IS A FRAMING FACT, NOT CONTENT: that a time charterer's commercial interest in efficiency and emissions performance now shapes speed and routing instructions. That is common ground with the CII family and is stated at one line, without importing any CII mechanism, rating or regulation.

EVERYTHING ELSE IS AUTHORED - the charterparty division of responsibility, all seven influences, the warranty and off-hire treatment, the whole pre-voyage assessment, the options ladder, the actions list and the ISM framing.

THIS IS THE REGULATORY LIMB.
PRIMARY: SOLAS chapter IX - the mandatory basis of the ISM Code.

COMMERCIAL CONTRACT PRACTICE (declared provenance class): time-charter forms of the NYPE type - the employment and indemnity clause, the description clause with its speed and consumption warranty, the off-hire clause, the bunker specification and trading limits. Described BY FUNCTION. No clause number is cited and no charterparty wording is quoted, because the forms exist in several editions and are amended by rider clauses in every fixture.

ENGINEERING JUDGEMENT AND CLASS/MAKER PRACTICE: the machinery consequences of prolonged low load, of frequent manoeuvring, and of fuel quality; the systemic causes tested for in a repeated-failure investigation; and the pre-departure proving programme. Mechanisms explained; no maker figure, interval or threshold asserted.

P2: MARPOL Annex VI named for the sulphur limits and emission control areas behind compliant-fuel changeover; ISO 8217 named as the fuel specification a bunker clause references. Neither is quoted; MIW holds no licensed copy of ISO 8217.
unresolved: NO INSTRUMENT GOVERNS WHAT A CHARTERER MAY INSTRUCT. The constraints are the charterparty as a commercial contract, the owner's obligation to provide a seaworthy ship, and the ISM Code. No regulation has been manufactured to govern charterer's instructions - PASTPAPER_PRODUCTION_PROTOCOL 2.1 applied.

Charterparty terms are described generically and by function. NYPE and the other standard forms exist in several editions with materially different wording and are amended by rider clauses in every fixture, so no clause number is cited and no wording is quoted. Whether a particular breakdown puts a particular ship off hire depends on the actual fixture, including whether it operates on a net-loss-of-time or a period basis, and no outcome is asserted.
MIW holds no licensed copy of ISO 8217. It is named as the specification a bunker clause normally references; no table, grade limit or parameter value is quoted from it.

NO FIGURES ARE QUOTED - no percentage of fuel saved by slow steaming, no consumption figure, no overhaul interval and no catalytic-fines threshold. All are engine, maker and installation specific; the mechanisms are described and the parameters named instead.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: Two limbs. The first is a discussion of how a time charterer's commercial control translates into machinery consequences. The second is a Chief Engineer scenario with TWO explicit demands - the options available and the actions to be taken - both bounded to the period BEFORE the voyage begins. The examiner is testing commercial literacy alongside engineering judgement, and specifically whether the candidate knows where technical advice stops and commercial negotiation begins.

quick_revision.recall_15s: On a time charter the owner keeps possession, crew and technical management; the charterer buys time and directs EMPLOYMENT. So his influence on machinery is indirect - speed orders giving prolonged low load and fouling, bunkers he supplies and their cat fines, a trading pattern of manoeuvres and starts, cargo demand for heating and reefers, trading limits forcing fuel changeover, and commercial pressure to defer immobilisation. Two clauses price it: the speed and consumption warranty, and the off-hire clause under which hire ceases for time lost by breakdown of machinery - which is why a history of auxiliary breakdown is a recurring off-hire exposure. Before sailing: establish the true condition from PMS, defect list, alarm logs and conditions of class, look for a SYSTEMIC cause, check fuel, critical spares and familiarisation. Options are sail as-is, sail with a restricted envelope, rectify before departure, defer sailing, or recommend she does not proceed. Actions regardless: written assessment to Company and DPA, defects into the SMS, brief the master, order spares, prove the systems, sample the bunkers, match the maintenance plan to the voyage. The ISM Code gives the master overriding authority.
critical_numbers: Time charter - owner keeps possession, crew and technical management; charterer directs employment
Off-hire - hire ceases for time lost by breakdown of machinery preventing full working

quick_revision.critical_regulation: ISM Code - the company is responsible for maintenance of the ship and equipment, must identify equipment and technical systems whose sudden operational failure may result in hazardous situations and provide measures to promote their reliability, and the master has overriding authority and responsibility to take any action he considers to be in the best interests of safety and pollution prevention. There is NO regulation governing what a charterer may instruct.
quick_revision.major_trap: Answering what you would do at sea when the machinery breaks down. The stem says PRIOR TO THE COMMENCEMENT OF VOYAGE. The second trap is merging the options with the actions when the stem asks for both separately, and omitting the two options candidates avoid naming - requesting deferment of sailing, and recommending she does not proceed. The third is inventing a regulation governing charterer's instructions; there is none.

understand_first: The charterer never touches a valve. That single fact organises the whole answer. On a time charter he has bought the ship's time and the right to say where she goes, what she loads and roughly how fast - and every one of those commercial decisions arrives in the engine room as a technical consequence somebody has to absorb. Slow steaming is a commercial decision that shows up as cold corrosion. A cheap bunker stem is a commercial decision that shows up as catalytic fines in the liners. A tight port rotation is a commercial decision that shows up as starting-air compressors running all night. And because hire stops when the machinery does, the owner and the Chief Engineer actually want the same thing, which is why a written, evidence-based assessment before departure is the most powerful instrument a Chief Engineer has. It is not a complaint - it is the argument that spending money now is cheaper than off-hire later.

blocks.h: 1. What a time charter is, and where the charterer's power comes from

blocks.p: Under a time charter the owner keeps possession, the crew and the technical management of the ship and hires out her earning capacity for a period. The charterer pays hire for time, not for cargo carried, and in return acquires the right to direct the ship's employment. The division is the key to the whole question and standard forms such as NYPE express it in an employment and indemnity clause: the master and crew, though the owner's servants, follow the charterer's orders as to employment of the vessel.

So the charterer commands where she goes, what she carries and, within limits, how fast; the owner remains responsible for seaworthiness, manning, maintenance, class and safe operation. The charterer's influence on machinery is therefore almost always indirect - exercised through commercial instructions whose engineering consequences fall on the Chief Engineer. He never orders a setting on the governor; he orders a speed, a port rotation and a bunker grade, and the machinery lives with the result.

blocks.h: 2. The charterer's influences on propulsion and other machinery

ul: Speed instructions. The most direct influence. Orders to slow steam or to run at an economical speed keep the main engine at prolonged low load, with the familiar consequences - fouling of the turbocharger and economiser, poor combustion and deposits, cold corrosion in the liners, exhaust temperature deviations, soot fires in the economiser and the need for auxiliary blowers. Orders to increase speed to make a laycan load the engine near its maximum continuous rating for extended periods.

Bunkers. Under most time charters the charterer supplies and pays for the fuel, and therefore chooses the supplier and the grade within the specification the charterparty allows. That decides the quality the plant must digest - viscosity, density, catalytic fines, sulphur content, stability and compatibility with what is already on board - and it drives purifier settings, filter loading, fuel-pump and injector wear, and changeover management.

Trading pattern and port rotation. Short passages with frequent port calls mean many manoeuvres, repeated starts and stops, high starting-air demand, more time on auxiliary power and less time at steady sea load. Long ballast legs, waiting at anchor and idle time bring their own problems of layup, standby machinery and lubrication.

Cargo-related demand. The cargo the charterer fixes determines the load on ancillary plant - cargo heating and the steam demand it creates, reefer containers and the electrical load, inert gas, tank cleaning and pumping, ballast exchange or treatment, and on some trades the cargo pumps and turbines as a major consumer.

Trading limits and voyage areas. Ice, tropical seawater temperature, high ambient, sediment-laden or biologically rich water for the ballast water treatment plant, and emission-control areas requiring compliant fuel changeover - all follow from the charterer's employment orders.

Time pressure on maintenance. The commercially valuable ship is the moving one. Pressure to defer immobilisation for overhauls, to shorten port stays and to postpone the withdrawal of a generator or a boiler is real and constant. It is exerted commercially, not by instruction, and it is the influence most likely to cause harm.

Efficiency and emissions performance. The charterer's commercial interest in the ship's rating and reported efficiency now shapes instructions on speed, routing, hull and propeller cleaning and voyage optimisation - a further reason for orders that keep the engine off its design point.

blocks.h: 3. Where the charterer's influence is priced - warranties and off-hire

blocks.p: Two clauses turn the Chief Engineer's plant into money, and he should know both.

ul: The description clause and the speed and consumption warranty. The owner warrants the ship's speed and fuel consumption in stated weather conditions. If she under-performs, the charterer claims the time lost and the fuel over-consumed. This is why accurate noon reports, weather data and consumption figures matter commercially as well as technically, and why a fouled hull, a slipping propeller or a mis-set engine becomes a dispute.

The off-hire clause. This is the one that bites on auxiliary breakdown. In the NYPE form, hire ceases for time lost by, among other things, breakdown of machinery, deficiency of men or stores, or damage preventing the full working of the vessel. The ship stops earning while she is unable to perform. A generator failure at sea that forces a speed reduction, or an immobilisation for repair, therefore converts directly into lost hire for the owner - and, where the charterparty is on a net loss of time basis, into an accounting argument about exactly how much time was lost.

blocks.p: That is the commercial reality behind the second half of this question. A history of unforeseen auxiliary breakdown at sea is not merely a technical nuisance; on a time charter it is a recurring off-hire exposure for the owner and a source of claims, and it is what makes the Chief Engineer's pre-voyage work valuable.

blocks.h: 4. Taking over the ship - establishing her true condition

blocks.p: Nothing useful can be decided before the plant's actual state is known, and a handover is the one moment when asking every question is expected. Prior to the voyage:

ol: Take a proper handover. A written handover from the outgoing Chief Engineer, and specifically his account of each auxiliary failure - what failed, what was done, and whether the cause was ever established.

Read the history rather than the last entry. The planned maintenance system - overdue jobs, jobs closed without work, running hours against overhaul intervals; the defect list and outstanding work orders; alarm and trip logs; the engine-room log for repeated abnormalities; previous superintendent and internal audit reports and any open non-conformities.

Establish the class and statutory position. Survey status, conditions of class or memoranda, overdue or postponed surveys, and the status of any equipment under a continuous survey cycle. A condition of class is a constraint on what may be deferred.

Look for the pattern. Repeated breakdown at sea of auxiliary machinery usually has a systemic cause rather than several coincidental ones - commonly fuel quality and treatment, cooling water chemistry or fouling, lubricating oil condition, electrical protection and load sharing, governor or automation faults, or simply maintenance not actually performed. Test the plant against each rather than repairing the last symptom.

Check the consumables and the fuel actually on board. Bunker delivery notes, retained samples, the latest fuel analysis - catalytic fines above all - the condition and settings of the purifiers, filter differential pressures and the compatibility of any blend.

Check spares and stores against the plant. Identification of critical equipment and the spares to support it is an ISM obligation, not a preference. Verify physical stock against the inventory, look at lead times, and identify the single points of failure with no spare on board.

Check the people. Familiarisation of newly joined engineers, competence for the specific plant, watchkeeping arrangements, and readiness for unmanned machinery space operation including alarm transfer and response times.

Read the charterparty extracts the company holds - the description and speed and consumption clause, the off-hire clause, the bunker specification and the trading limits - so that the technical advice given is framed in the terms that will actually be applied.

blocks.h: 5. The options, and what each one means

blocks.p: Having established the condition, the realistic options range from acceptance to refusal, and the Chief Engineer should present them as a recommendation with consequences rather than as a complaint:

ol: Sail as she is, where the investigation shows the failures were addressed and the cause is understood. Legitimate only if it can be justified on evidence.

Sail with mitigation and a restricted operating envelope - additional condition monitoring, more frequent inspections, redundancy preserved by running an extra generator on critical passages, load limits, avoidance of the conditions that provoked the failure. Record the restriction and tell the master and the company.

Rectify before departure - carry out the outstanding work alongside or at anchorage, with maker's or specialist attendance and, where the defect touches a classed item, class attendance. Ask the company for a superintendent.
Request a deferment of sailing, or of the fixture, until a specific defect is rectified. This is the option candidates avoid naming, and it is a proper one.

Recommend that the vessel not proceed where the plant cannot be made fit for the intended voyage. The master's overriding authority under the ISM Code exists for exactly this, and the Chief Engineer's role is to give him the technical basis for using it.

blocks.h: 6. Actions prior to commencement of the voyage

ul: Put the assessment in writing to the Company and the DPA. A verbal concern is not a record. State the defect, the risk, the option recommended and what is needed - it is also the mechanism by which the ISM system is supposed to work, and it moves the decision to the level that can fund it.
Raise the outstanding items formally in the safety management system as defects or non-conformities so they are tracked rather than remembered.

Brief the master fully, in terms of operational consequence rather than machinery detail - what she can and cannot do, what the plant will not tolerate, and what he should not accept in an employment order.
Order the critical spares and press for delivery before departure; where they cannot arrive in time, say so explicitly in the written assessment.

Test and prove the essential systems before sailing - generators on load and in parallel, automatic start of the standby set, blackout recovery and the emergency generator, steering gear, main engine trials and reversing, the emergency fire pump, bilge and ballast systems, boiler safety devices and alarm transfer.
Sample and analyse the bunkers before use, and do not use a stem of doubtful compatibility on a critical passage while the result is outstanding.

Set the maintenance plan against the actual voyage - schedule immobilisation and heavy work for ports where it is feasible, and agree it with the master and the company in advance so it is not competing with a fixture later.
Bring the crew into it. Brief the engineers on the failure history and the watch response; run drills for blackout and for the specific failure mode seen before.

Keep the commercial and technical roles separate. The Chief Engineer advises on the ship's technical condition; he does not negotiate with the charterer, accept employment orders, or comment on hire and off-hire. Those are the master's and the owner's. Where pressure to sail is applied, record it, refer it to the company, and let the master's overriding authority operate.

blocks.h: 7. The line the Chief Engineer must not let be crossed

blocks.p: A charterer may direct employment. He may not direct unsafe operation, and no charterparty instruction overrides the owner's obligation to provide a seaworthy, properly maintained ship or the master's authority to refuse. The ISM Code makes the company responsible for the ship's maintenance and for supporting the master, and gives the master overriding authority and responsibility to take any action he considers in the best interests of safety and pollution prevention. The practical discipline is simple: let the commercial pressure be answered commercially and the engineering question answered on engineering evidence, and put the engineering answer in writing before the ship sails, not after she breaks down.

Two limbs, and the second is longer than it looks. The first asks for the influences of a charterer on machinery operation - a discussion. The second is a scenario with two explicit demands: state the different option you have and actions you would takes, both prior to the commencement of voyage. That is three things to head, not two, and options and actions are not the same list - options are the courses open to you, actions are what you do regardless of which you choose. Candidates who merge them lose the marks for the one they left out. The words prior to the commencement of voyage also bound the answer: describing how you would fix a generator at sea does not answer this question.

blocks.h: The idea that makes limb one coherent

blocks.p: The charterer never touches the machinery. On a time charter the owner keeps possession, crew and technical management; the charterer buys the ship's time and directs her employment. So every influence in limb one is indirect - a commercial instruction with an engineering consequence. He orders a speed, and the Chief Engineer gets prolonged low load, fouling and cold corrosion. He buys the bunkers, and the Chief Engineer gets the catalytic fines. He fixes a short-sea trade, and the Chief Engineer gets manoeuvres and starting-air demand. Saying that once, at the top, turns a shopping list into an argument - and it is also the sentence that sets up limb two, because it explains why the pre-voyage assessment is the Chief Engineer's real point of leverage.

blocks.h: Know the two clauses that convert engineering into money

blocks.p: At management level the examiner expects commercial literacy. Two clauses do the work. The speed and consumption warranty in the description clause exposes the owner to a claim for time lost and fuel over-consumed if the ship under-performs - which is why noon reports and consumption figures are commercially live documents. The off-hire clause is the one that matters for this scenario: hire ceases for time lost by breakdown of machinery, deficiency of men or stores, or damage preventing the full working of the vessel. A history of unforeseen auxiliary breakdown at sea is therefore a recurring off-hire exposure, not merely a technical nuisance, and naming that is what shows you understand why the company should fund the repairs you are about to ask for.

blocks.h: Options and actions - keep them apart

blocks.p: Set the options out as a ladder with consequences: sail as she is; sail with mitigation and a restricted operating envelope; rectify before departure with maker's or class attendance; request deferment of sailing; recommend that she not proceed. Name the last two. Candidates instinctively avoid them because they sound like refusing to work, but they are proper professional options and the master's overriding authority under the ISM Code exists precisely so that they can be exercised. Then the actions - written assessment to the Company and DPA, defects raised in the SMS, master briefed, critical spares ordered, systems proved before sailing, bunkers sampled, maintenance plan matched to the voyage, crew briefed and drilled. Those you do whichever option is chosen.

ul: Writing about a voyage charter or a bareboat charter. The stem says time charter, and the division of responsibility is what the question turns on.
Saying the charterer instructs the Chief Engineer on machinery. He does not - he directs employment, and the machinery consequences follow.
Merging options and actions into one list when the stem asks for both.
Answering what you would do at sea when it breaks down. The stem says prior to the commencement of voyage.
Omitting off-hire entirely. It is the clause that makes auxiliary breakdown expensive and it is the commercial hinge of the scenario.
Treating each past breakdown as an isolated event instead of looking for the systemic cause - fuel, cooling, lube oil, electrical protection, automation, or maintenance not actually done.
Forgetting conditions of class and survey status, which constrain what may legitimately be deferred.
Not putting anything in writing. A verbal concern is not a record and does not move the decision to the company.
Straying into the commercial role - negotiating with the charterer, or opining on hire. That is the master's and the owner's ground.
Inventing a regulation that governs charterer's instructions. There is none; the constraints are the charterparty, the ISM Code and the owner's obligation to provide a seaworthy ship.

blocks.p: "The charterer has ordered slow steaming. Can you refuse?" Not as a commercial order - speed is employment. But you advise on the technical consequences, agree load limits and countermeasures, and if prolonged low load would endanger the plant or the ship you say so in writing and the master decides. "The charterer's bunkers are off-specification. Whose problem?" The charterparty allocates it, but the immediate engineering decision is yours - do not burn a doubtful stem on a critical passage while the analysis is outstanding. "The company says sail, you say the generator is unfit." Put the technical assessment in writing to the Company and the DPA and brief the master; the ISM Code gives the master overriding authority. "Is a generator breakdown off-hire?" Under a typical NYPE off-hire clause, time lost by breakdown of machinery preventing the full working of the vessel is - but it is the master's and owner's ground to argue, not yours.

ul: What does a time charterer actually control? Employment - where she goes, what she carries, and within limits how fast. Not possession, crew or technical management.
Who buys the bunkers on a time charter? Normally the charterer, within the specification the charterparty allows.
What is off-hire? A clause under which hire ceases for time lost by breakdown of machinery, deficiency of men or stores, or damage preventing the full working of the vessel.
What is the speed and consumption warranty? The owner's warranted performance in stated weather; under-performance exposes him to a claim for time lost and fuel over-consumed.

Give three machinery consequences of prolonged slow steaming. Turbocharger and economiser fouling, poor combustion and deposits, cold corrosion of liners; also auxiliary blower running and soot fires.

What would you look at first on taking over a ship with a breakdown history? The PMS - overdue jobs, jobs closed without work, running hours against overhaul intervals - then the defect list, alarm and trip logs, and conditions of class.
What is a condition of class? A requirement imposed by the society to be completed by a stated date; it constrains what can be deferred.
Which spares must be on board? Those supporting identified critical equipment, under the ISM Code.
Who can refuse to sail? The master, under his overriding authority in the ISM Code. The Chief Engineer supplies the technical basis.

blocks.p: For limb one, S - B - T - C - L - M: Speed, Bunkers, Trading pattern, Cargo demand, Limits and areas, Maintenance pressure (step 2), then the two clauses that price it (step 3). For limb two, FIND - CHOOSE - DO: find the true condition (step 4), choose among the options (step 5), and do the actions regardless of the choice (step 6).

ul: ISM Code - the company's responsibility for maintenance of the ship and equipment; identification of critical equipment and systems whose sudden failure may result in a hazardous situation, with measures to promote reliability; familiarisation of newly joined personnel; reporting of non-conformities, accidents and hazardous occurrences; and the master's overriding authority and responsibility to take any action he considers in the best interests of safety and pollution prevention. This is the regulatory limb of the answer.
SOLAS chapter IX - the mandatory basis of the ISM Code.
Classification society rules - survey status, conditions of class and memoranda; continuous survey cycles. Class technical material, not an IMO instrument.

NYPE and similar time-charter forms - the employment and indemnity clause, the description and speed and consumption warranty, the off-hire clause, the bunker specification and trading limits. Commercial contract practice, not regulation - see the uncertainty note.
ISO 8217 - the marine fuel specification a charterparty bunker clause normally references. Named; MIW holds no licensed copy and no clause of it is quoted.
MARPOL Annex VI - the sulphur limits and emission control areas behind compliant-fuel changeover, named as the reason a trading area drives a fuel decision.

blocks.p: Most of this question has no regulatory source, and that is stated rather than disguised. No instrument governs what a charterer may instruct - the constraints are the charterparty, which is a commercial contract between owner and charterer, the owner's obligation to provide a seaworthy ship, and the ISM Code. `PASTPAPER_PRODUCTION_PROTOCOL.md` §2.1 governs the charterparty and engineering limbs: the mechanisms are explained, the provenance class is declared, and no regulation has been manufactured to govern charterer's instructions.

Charterparty terms are described generically and by function. NYPE and the other standard forms exist in several editions with materially different wording, and their terms are amended by rider clauses in every fixture. No clause number is cited and no charterparty wording is quoted; the employment clause, the speed and consumption warranty and the off-hire clause are described by what they do. Whether a particular breakdown puts a particular ship off hire depends on the actual wording of the actual fixture - including whether it operates on a net-loss-of-time or a period basis - and the answer says so rather than asserting an outcome.

The regulatory limb is separable and is treated to the higher standard. The ISM Code obligations - maintenance of the ship and equipment, identification of critical equipment, familiarisation, reporting, and the master's overriding authority - are genuine requirements and are the ones the answer relies on when it says the Chief Engineer's route is a written assessment to the Company and the DPA.

No figures are quoted. No percentage of fuel saved by slow steaming, no consumption figure, no interval for any overhaul and no threshold for catalytic fines is asserted, because all of them are engine, maker and installation specific. The mechanisms are described and the parameters named - §2.1 applied, an unverifiable quantity omitted rather than given false precision.

blocks.h: The one connection worth making on this paper

blocks.p: Read this against Q8 on this paper. Both ask what happens when a ship is not fit to do what she is being asked to do - here the pressure is commercial and the safeguard is the master's overriding authority and a written assessment; there the pressure is regulatory and the safeguard is a port State detention. The two questions approach the same defect from opposite directions, and the same discipline answers both: establish the condition on evidence, record it in writing, and do not let the decision be made by whoever is in the greatest hurry.

retrieval_cards.prompt: On a time charter, what does the charterer actually control?
retrieval_cards.answer: Employment - where the ship goes, what she carries and within limits how fast. The owner keeps possession, the crew and technical management, and remains responsible for seaworthiness, manning, maintenance, class and safe operation. The employment and indemnity clause in forms such as NYPE provides that the master and crew, though the owner's servants, follow the charterer's orders as to employment of the vessel.
retrieval_cards.why: The division of responsibility is what the whole question turns on.

retrieval_cards.prompt: List the ways a time charterer influences machinery operation.
retrieval_cards.answer: Speed instructions, producing prolonged low load or extended running near maximum continuous rating. Bunkers, since the charterer supplies and chooses the grade and quality within the charterparty specification. Trading pattern and port rotation, driving manoeuvres, starts and stops and idle time. Cargo demand - heating, reefers, inert gas, tank cleaning, ballast and cargo pumps. Trading limits and areas, including ice, high ambient and emission control areas. Commercial pressure to defer immobilisation for maintenance. And efficiency and emissions performance shaping speed and routing.
retrieval_cards.why: Limb one is a list, and it should be a structured one.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Does the charterer instruct the Chief Engineer on how to run the machinery?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. On a time charter he directs employment, not technical management, and his influence on machinery is indirect - a commercial instruction with an engineering consequence. He orders a speed, a port rotation and a bunker grade; the machinery consequences fall to the Chief Engineer. He may direct employment but may not direct unsafe operation, and no charterparty instruction overrides the owner's obligation to provide a seaworthy ship or the master's overriding authority.
retrieval_cards.why: Getting the direction of influence wrong undermines the whole answer.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the off-hire clause and why does it matter to a Chief Engineer?
retrieval_cards.answer: A clause under which hire ceases for time lost by, among other things, breakdown of machinery, deficiency of men or stores, or damage preventing the full working of the vessel. It matters because it converts an auxiliary breakdown at sea directly into lost hire for the owner, so a history of unforeseen breakdowns is a recurring commercial exposure and not merely a technical nuisance. Whether a given failure puts the ship off hire depends on the actual fixture wording, including whether it operates on a net-loss-of-time or a period basis.
retrieval_cards.why: The commercial hinge of the scenario, and the argument for funding the repairs.

retrieval_cards.prompt: You take over a ship with a history of unforeseen auxiliary breakdown at sea. What do you examine first?
retrieval_cards.answer: The history rather than the last entry. A written handover with the outgoing Chief's account of each failure and whether a cause was ever established; the planned maintenance system for overdue jobs, jobs closed without work and running hours against overhaul intervals; the defect list and open work orders; alarm and trip logs; audit non-conformities; and the class survey status including any conditions of class. Then look for a systemic cause rather than repairing the last symptom.
retrieval_cards.why: Repeated failures of the same class usually share one cause.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What systemic causes should be tested for repeated auxiliary breakdowns at sea?
retrieval_cards.answer: Fuel quality and treatment, including catalytic fines, purifier settings and compatibility of blends; cooling water chemistry or fouling; lubricating oil condition; electrical protection and load sharing; governor or automation faults; and maintenance recorded but not actually performed. Test the plant against each rather than treating the failures as coincidental.
retrieval_cards.why: The examiner wants diagnosis, not a repair narrative.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State the options open to a Chief Engineer before sailing.
retrieval_cards.answer: Sail as she is, where the investigation shows the cause is understood and addressed. Sail with mitigation and a restricted operating envelope - extra condition monitoring, preserved redundancy, load limits - recorded and notified. Rectify before departure with maker's, superintendent or class attendance. Request a deferment of sailing until a specific defect is rectified. Or recommend that the vessel not proceed, the master's overriding authority under the ISM Code existing for exactly that.
retrieval_cards.why: The stem asks for options separately from actions, and the last two are the ones candidates omit.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What actions do you take before departure regardless of which option is chosen?
retrieval_cards.answer: Put the assessment in writing to the Company and the DPA; raise outstanding items formally in the safety management system; brief the master in terms of operational consequence; order critical spares and state explicitly if they cannot arrive in time; prove the essential systems - generators in parallel, standby start, blackout recovery, emergency generator, steering gear, main engine trials, emergency fire pump; sample and analyse the bunkers before use; match the maintenance plan to the actual voyage and agree it in advance; and brief and drill the engineers on the failure history.
retrieval_cards.why: Actions and options are two separate demands in the stem.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does the ISM Code contribute to this situation?
retrieval_cards.answer: It is the regulatory limb. The company is responsible for maintenance of the ship and equipment and must identify critical equipment and systems whose sudden failure may result in a hazardous situation, with measures to promote their reliability. It requires familiarisation of newly joined personnel and the reporting of non-conformities, accidents and hazardous occurrences. And it gives the master overriding authority and responsibility to take any action he considers in the best interests of safety and pollution prevention.
retrieval_cards.why: Everything else in the answer is contract or judgement; this is the requirement.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which regulation governs what a charterer may instruct?
retrieval_cards.answer: None. There is no instrument governing charterer's instructions. The constraints are the charterparty, which is a commercial contract between owner and charterer; the owner's obligation to provide a seaworthy and properly maintained ship; and the ISM Code, which places maintenance and support of the master on the company and gives the master overriding authority. Inventing a regulation here would be a serious error.
retrieval_cards.why: Protocol 2.1 - declare the provenance rather than manufacture a rule.

verification_status: Authored this session, fully fresh. Protocol 2.1 applied to the charterparty and engineering limbs with the provenance class declared; the ISM regulatory limb kept separable and verified. Full temporal and internal Q-reference sweeps run.

notes: NO TEMPORAL COMPONENT IN THE DOMINANT LIMBS. The time-charter division of responsibility, the off-hire concept, the speed and consumption warranty and the machinery consequences of low load and poor fuel are settled commercial and engineering ground with no entry-into-force date. The intake recorded STABLE / LOW and that is confirmed.
THE REGULATORY LIMB WAS CHECKED AGAINST THE SITTING. The ISM Code, mandatory through SOLAS chapter IX, was in force at December 2025 and nothing relied on here moved before it.

THE ONE MOVING ELEMENT WAS DELIBERATELY GENERALISED. The commercial pressure created by a ship's efficiency and emissions performance is real and is stated at one line, but NO rating scheme, threshold, band, year or regulation is named - because that material moves and because it belongs to a different question. This also keeps the CII family's content out of an answer that does not set it.

THE 34TH ASSEMBLY BOUNDARY IS CHECKED AND NOT ENGAGED. No A.12xx resolution of any session is cited. The instruments named are the ISM Code, SOLAS chapter IX and MARPOL Annex VI, none on the Assembly re-issue cycle. Negative finding, recorded.

THE INDIAN STATUTE BOUNDARY DOES NOT REACH THIS QUESTION. Neither Merchant Shipping Act is cited; the stem sets no Indian limb and none was added. Checked because two other questions on this paper turn on it.

THE IMO NET-ZERO FRAMEWORK IS NOT MENTIONED ANYWHERE, and that is deliberate. It was approved but NOT adopted and not in force at this sitting, and a question about charterers and fuel is precisely where it would have been tempting to introduce it.
